meta.status: 2026 budget final (approved by City Council 2026-02-10). 2027 budget not yet released.
meta.units: Program figures are in millions of dollars ($M) unless noted.
meta.netDefinition: Net budget = what a program spends (gross) minus its own revenue (fares, provincial/federal grants, user fees). The net amount is what the City must cover from property tax and city-wide revenues such as the land transfer tax.

propertyTax.assessmentHelp: From your MPAC notice. Toronto still uses 2016 values; the average home is assessed at $692,140.

meta.budgetProcess: Under Ontario's 'strong mayor' rules the Mayor proposes the budget, Council can amend it, the Mayor can veto amendments, and Council needs a two-thirds vote to override.
meta.methodNote: Figures come from City of Toronto budget documents (Budget Notes, the Mayor's Budget Report, Council decisions) and service reports, cross-checked against news coverage. Program figures are net operating budgets: the part paid by City revenue after each program's own fares, fees and grants. The 13 services shown are the large, resident-facing ones; the full budget also includes debt payments, corporate accounts and smaller divisions. Per-household figures divide by the number of private households (2021 Census) to give a sense of scale; they are not what any one household pays.

programs.name: TTC (transit)
programs.what: Subway, streetcar, bus and Wheel-Trans service.
programs.basisNote: Reported as roughly $1.48B net, about $94M more than 2025. 2025 recommended net was $1.387B.
highlights: Fares frozen for a third straight year.
Fare cap: ride free after 47 paid rides a month starting September 2026; planned to drop to 40 rides in 2027.
$35.0M drawn from a TTC reserve to cover $34.4M in lower-than-expected fare revenue.
$1.8M pilot putting Toronto Community Crisis Service workers on the TTC.

outcomes.metric: Ridership compared with before the pandemic
outcomes.note: Measured on slightly different bases (point in time vs. year to date), so treat the gain as approximate. Peer systems averaged about 84%.

programs.name: Toronto Police Service
highlights: $50.7M for the new police collective agreement (pay raises).
$20.5M for the multi-year hiring plan (360 officers hired in 2026; about 143 net new after retirements).

outcomes.metric: Average response to the most urgent (Priority 1) calls
outcomes.note: 2025 figure from the Chief's Annual Report, which reports a 17.5% drop; 2024 calculated from that. Down from a 23.1-minute average in 2023. No 2026 figure published yet.

programs.name: Paramedic Services
programs.basisNote: 2026 net from Budget Notes; 2025 calculated from the reported +$34.929M (+24.9%) change.
highlights: Largest percentage increase of any major program (+24.9%).
Part of 258 new emergency-services positions aimed at faster response times.

outcomes.note: Up 22% since 2019, and fewer than 10% of ambulances were free for about 4 hours a day on average. The 2026 money (94 new positions) is meant to improve this; no 2026 result is published yet.

programs.name: Fire Services
programs.what: Firefighting, rescue, fire prevention and inspections.
programs.basisNote: 2026 net $558.9M from Budget Notes; 2025 calculated from the reported +1.8% change.
highlights: $41M in the capital plan for equipment, including two new high-rise trucks.

programs.name: Shelter & Support Services
programs.what: Emergency shelters, encampment response, drop-ins, homelessness prevention.
programs.basisNote: 2026 net from Budget Notes; 2025 calculated from the reported +$15.266M (+6.9%) change.
highlights: $200M drawn from a shelter reserve to cover provincial funding expected under the City-Province 'New Deal'.
Council added $0.1M for drop-in centre supplies.

outcomes.metric: People who called for a shelter bed and couldn't get one, per night
outcomes.note: Average of 30.4 (Jan) and 32.8 (Feb). Counts single adults and couples only; families are not included, so real unmet need is higher. About 9,200 people a night were in shelters.

programs.name: Housing Secretariat
programs.what: Affordable housing programs, rent supports, social housing administration.
programs.basisNote: 2026 net from Budget Notes; 2025 calculated from the reported +$15.759M (+2.7%) change.
highlights: Council moved $0.185M toward legal services in the Toronto Tenant Support Program.

programs.name: Toronto Community Housing (City funding)
programs.what: City operating subsidy to Canada's largest social housing landlord.
programs.basisNote: City operating funding to TCHC per Budget Notes ($329.985M, +$2.519M).
highlights: $5.9M of subsidy shifted from Toronto Seniors Housing to TCHC (no change to the total).

programs.name: Employment & Social Services
programs.what: Ontario Works (social assistance) delivery and employment help.
programs.basisNote: 2025 and 2026 nets from each year's Budget Notes / Council decision. Change calculated.

programs.name: Children's Services
programs.what: Child care subsidies, $10-a-day child care system management.
programs.basisNote: 2026 net from Budget Notes; 2025 calculated from the reported +$1.817M (+1.8%) change.
highlights: Gross spending (mostly provincial/federal child-care money) falls about 5.7%, from roughly $1.68B to $1.58B, even as the City's own share rises slightly.

programs.name: Toronto Public Health
programs.what: Disease prevention, inspections, student nutrition, harm reduction.
programs.basisNote: 2026 net from Program Summary; 2025 calculated from the reported +10.1% change.
highlights: Student Nutrition Program expanded: about 330,000 students a day in 841 schools (roughly 62,000 more students, 155 more schools).

programs.name: Toronto Public Library
programs.what: 100 library branches, programs and digital services.
programs.basisNote: 2026 net from Budget Notes; 2025 calculated from the reported +$19.834M (+7.8%) change.
highlights: All 100 branches open 7 days a week by summer 2026 (17 more branches added to the Open Hours Plan).
Social and crisis support workers expanded to 4 more branches.

outcomes.metric: Sunday visits after all branches opened Sundays
outcomes.note: Result of the 2025 Sunday-hours expansion, which the 2026 budget extends to seven days a week.

programs.name: Parks & Recreation
programs.what: Parks, community centres, pools, rinks, recreation programs.
programs.basisNote: 2026 net from Budget Notes; 2025 calculated from the reported +$19.9M (+5.6%) change.

programs.name: Transportation Services
programs.what: Roads, sidewalks, traffic signals, snow clearing, cycling infrastructure.
programs.basisNote: 2026 net from Budget Notes; 2025 calculated from the reported -$25.046M (-7.6%) change.
highlights: The only major program in this list whose City-funded (net) budget went down. The sources we could reach do not explain why; a drop in net can come from cuts or from new revenue (e.g. fees, provincial funding), so check the Budget Notes before calling this a service cut.

gapClosing.note: The City reported a $1.34B gap between what it would cost to keep services running and the revenue it expected. A gap that size would have needed a ~27% property tax increase on its own. The measures below are as reported by different sources and overlap (for example, efficiencies are part of 'reductions and offsets'), so they should not be added together.

measures.label: Reductions & offsets (all kinds)
measures.detail: Mayor's office total for spending reductions and offsetting revenue.

measures.label: Extra reserve draws vs. 2025
measures.detail: Roughly $400M more taken from City savings (reserves) than the year before. About 9% of the 2026 budget is funded from reserves.

measures.label: Temporary 'bridging' from reserves
measures.detail: One-time reserve money that has to be replaced in future years.

measures.label: Shelter reserve draw
measures.detail: Covers provincial funding the City expects under the 'New Deal' but has not yet received.

measures.label: Line-by-line reviews & hiring freeze
measures.detail: Savings from reviewing each division's spending, plus a freeze on non-essential (non-frontline) hiring that continues through 2026.

measures.label: Permanent efficiencies
measures.detail: Ongoing savings from process, technology and staffing changes.

measures.label: TTC reserve draw
measures.detail: Keeps fares frozen while fare revenue comes in $34.4M lower than planned.

revenue.note: Approximate. Shares come from news and City summaries that use slightly different bases; 'Everything else' is the remainder needed to reach the $18.9B total.

parts.label: Everything else (water & garbage rates, TTC fares, user fees, other)

utilityRates.note: Single-family annual solid waste fees. 2025 fee derived by removing the 3.75% increase; matches the City's published $11.49–$21.97 increase range.

capital.note: Largest 10-year capital plan in City history (2026–2035). Over half goes to repairing what already exists. $31.7B of transit expansion is not funded.
capital.unfundedLabel: Transit expansion projects with no money attached yet

inYear.note: Snapshot from the City's first 2026 operating variance report (four months). Negative = projected overspend / shortfall by year-end. Later reports may differ.

timeline.label: Oct 2025
timeline.title: Public budget consultations
timeline.detail: City asks residents for input before staff build the budget.

timeline.label: Dec 2025
timeline.title: Water & garbage rates set
timeline.detail: Council approves 3.75% increases to water and solid waste rates, ahead of the main budget.

timeline.label: Dec 10, 2025
timeline.title: Police board approves $1.43B request
timeline.detail: The Police Service Board approves a 7% increase. Council still has to fund it.

timeline.label: Jan 1, 2026
timeline.title: New water & garbage rates take effect

timeline.label: Jan 8, 2026
timeline.title: Staff budget launched
timeline.detail: City staff release the $18.9B budget with a 2.2% tax increase and a $1.34B gap to close.

timeline.label: Feb 2, 2026
timeline.title: Mayor's budget tabled
timeline.detail: Under Ontario's 'strong mayor' rules the Mayor, not Council, proposes the budget. Chow keeps the 2.2% increase and adds money for youth safety and homeless outreach.

timeline.label: Feb 10, 2026
timeline.title: Council approves the budget
timeline.detail: Council can amend the Mayor's budget (the Mayor can veto; Council needs two-thirds to override). Council adds $2M in service enhancements; tax increase passes 19–5.

timeline.label: Apr 30, 2026
timeline.title: First check-up: $97.4M shortfall projected
timeline.detail: Four months in, the City projects ending the year $97.4M over budget on tax-supported services; the TTC alone projects $64.3M.

timeline.label: Summer 2026
timeline.title: All libraries open 7 days a week (planned)
timeline.detail: Target date for all 100 branches to open seven days a week. Completion not yet confirmed publicly.

timeline.label: Sep 2026
timeline.title: TTC fare cap begins (47 rides)
timeline.detail: Took effect September 1, 2026: after 47 paid rides in a calendar month, the rest of the month's rides are free. Monthly passes ended August 31.

timeline.label: Oct 26, 2026
timeline.title: Municipal election
timeline.detail: Olivia Chow re-elected mayor (about 54% of the vote) over Brad Bradford.

timeline.label: Jan 2027 (expected)
timeline.title: 2027 staff budget launch
timeline.detail: Expected based on the 2026 calendar. Opening gap estimated at $1.1B–$1.5B.

timeline.label: By Feb 1, 2027 (expected)
timeline.title: Mayor's 2027 budget
timeline.detail: The Mayor must table a budget by February 1 under strong-mayor rules; Council then has 30 days to amend.

timeline.title: Fare cap planned to drop to 40 rides
timeline.detail: Part of the multi-year fare-capping plan approved in the 2026 budget.

commitments.promise: Freeze TTC fares for 2026 (third year in a row)
Monthly fare cap: free rides after 47 paid trips, starting September 2026
commitments.evidence: Fare capping took effect September 1, 2026, on PRESTO and debit/credit tap.

commitments.promise: All 100 library branches open 7 days a week by July 2026
commitments.evidence: Planned for July 2026 (June 2026 library report still listed it as upcoming). We found no public confirmation it was completed.

commitments.promise: Expand student nutrition to about 330,000 students a day in 841 schools
commitments.evidence: Funded in the final budget. No delivery report found yet.

commitments.promise: Hire 360 police officers in 2026 (about 143 net new)
commitments.evidence: Funded ($20.5M). No year-end hiring report yet.

commitments.promise: Add 94 permanent paramedic positions to improve response times
commitments.evidence: Funded ($15.2M gross, $7.0M net). No 2026 response-time results published yet.

commitments.promise: Deliver services within the approved budget
commitments.evidence: As of April 30, the City projected a $97.4M overspend on tax-supported services (TTC: $64.3M).

commitments.promise: Lower the fare cap to 40 rides a month in 2027
commitments.evidence: Planned for 2027; depends on the 2027 budget.

points: The City's own outlook projected about a $1.1B shortfall going into 2027.
Including expected reductions in provincial and federal funding, City Hall columnist Matt Elliott estimates about $1.5B.
$323M of 2026 'bridging' money from reserves was one-time and must be replaced.
The TTC fare cap is planned to drop from 47 to 40 rides a month in 2027, which costs fare revenue.
Mayor Olivia Chow was re-elected on October 26, 2026, so the 2027 budget will again be a 'strong mayor' budget she proposes.

taxHistoryNote: 2026 was an election year; its increase was the smallest of the current mayor's term.
